title: What Causes Musculoskeletal Pain?

items.text: Nociceptive — direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury
items.md: Nociceptive — direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury

items.text: Inflammatory — pain driven by inflammatory mediators
items.md: Inflammatory — pain driven by inflammatory mediators

items.text: Neuropathic — pain from nerve injury or dysfunction
items.md: Neuropathic — pain from nerve injury or dysfunction

items.text: Acute — recent onset, often tied to identifiable injury or flare
items.md: Acute — recent onset, often tied to identifiable injury or flare

items.text: Chronic — persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months
items.md: Chronic — persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months

items.text: Treatment approach differs sharply between the two
items.md: Treatment approach differs sharply between the two

notes:
Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory — pure neuropathic pain is more the territory of a separate pharmacology unit.

Say: "Pain is classified by mechanism (nociceptive, inflammatory, neuropathic) and by time (acute vs. chronic)."

title: Inflammation Drives Pain

items.text: Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.

emphasis.text: Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.

items.md: **Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.**

notes:
This mediator list is the roadmap for the whole lecture — NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

Say: "Injury releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine and cytokines. These lower the nociceptor threshold, so normally harmless stimuli hurt."

title: Inflammatory Mediators Sensitize Nociceptors

items.text: Injury releases mediators: PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines.
items.md: **Injury releases mediators:**  PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines.

items.text: Nociceptor sensitization: mediators lower the pain threshold.
items.md: **Nociceptor sensitization:**  mediators lower the pain threshold.

items.text: Where drugs act: NSAIDs block COX; corticosteroids block PLA2 upstream.
items.md: **Where drugs act:**  NSAIDs block COX; corticosteroids block PLA2 upstream.

notes:
Say: "Injury releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine and cytokines. These lower the nociceptor threshold, so normally harmless stimuli hurt."

Know: Prostaglandins sensitize nociceptors, so they are the main NSAID target.

Know: Bradykinin, histamine and cytokines are not blocked by NSAIDs.

Say: "That's the pathway. Now the simplest drug on it: acetaminophen."

title: Acetaminophen

items.text: ●  Analgesic effect: relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.
items.md: **●  Analgesic effect:** relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.

items.text: ●  Antipyretic effect: reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.
items.md: **●  Antipyretic effect:** reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.

items.text: ●  Anti-inflammatory effect: minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.
items.md: **●  Anti-inflammatory effect:** minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.

notes:
This is the single most important distinction students need: acetaminophen treats pain and fever well, but it is not an anti-inflammatory drug the way NSAIDs are.

Say: "Acetaminophen is mainly central, with analgesic and antipyretic effects and minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory action."

Know: It is not an anti-inflammatory drug.

title: Acetaminophen: Safe vs. Toxic Metabolism

items.text: Mechanism: analgesia and antipyresis are mainly central via reduced CNS prostaglandin synthesis; peripheral anti-inflammatory action is minimal.
items.md: **Mechanism:**  analgesia and antipyresis are mainly central via reduced CNS prostaglandin synthesis; peripheral anti-inflammatory action is minimal.

items.text: Major route: glucuronidation and sulfation handle about 90% of the dose, giving safe urinary excretion.
items.md: **Major route:**  glucuronidation and sulfation handle about 90% of the dose, giving safe urinary excretion.

items.text: Minor route: CYP2E1 converts a small fraction to NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine), normally neutralized by glutathione.
items.md: **Minor route:**  CYP2E1 converts a small fraction to NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine), normally neutralized by glutathione.

items.text: GSH conjugation → safe excretion (at therapeutic doses)
items.md: GSH conjugation → safe excretion (at therapeutic doses)

notes:
Explain the major safe route first, then the minor CYP2E1 route, where NAPQI is normally neutralized by glutathione conjugation at therapeutic doses.

Say: "About 90% goes down the safe route of glucuronidation and sulfation. A small fraction goes through CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which glutathione neutralizes at normal doses."

title: Acetaminophen Overdose and NAC Rescue

items.text: Overdose: glutathione is exhausted, so NAPQI injures hepatocytes.
items.md: **Overdose:**  glutathione is exhausted, so NAPQI injures hepatocytes.

items.text: Antidote: NAC replenishes glutathione; give early for best effect.
items.md: **Antidote:**  NAC replenishes glutathione; give early for best effect.

items.text: Pearl: chronic alcohol use and fasting lower GSH and raise risk; both also induce CYP2E1.
items.md: **Pearl:**  chronic alcohol use and fasting lower GSH and raise risk; both also induce CYP2E1.

items.text: Monitoring: plot the acetaminophen level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for acute single ingestion; check AST/ALT.
items.md: **Monitoring:**  plot the acetaminophen level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for acute single ingestion; check AST/ALT.

notes:
Overdose saturates glucuronidation and sulfation, shunting more drug to CYP2E1 and producing more NAPQI. Once glutathione is depleted, NAPQI injures hepatocytes. Give N-acetylcysteine early.

Say: "In overdose the safe route saturates, more drug goes to CYP2E1, glutathione runs out, and NAPQI injures hepatocytes."

Know: The antidote is N-acetylcysteine (NAC), given early.

Know: Chronic alcohol use and fasting raise the risk.

Know: Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for acute single ingestions, and check AST/ALT.

title: Rumack-Matthew Nomogram: Assessing Toxicity

items.text: How to use: draw a level at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion and plot it against time since ingestion.
items.md: **How to use:**  draw a level at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion and plot it against time since ingestion.

items.text: Above the treatment line: give NAC.
Limits: not valid before 4 hours, for unknown ingestion time, staggered or repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, or chronic use; treat these using clinical judgment, AST/ALT and poison control.
items.md: **Limits:**  not valid before 4 hours, for unknown ingestion time, staggered or repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, or chronic use; treat these using clinical judgment, AST/ALT and poison control.

items.text: Example: 8 h, 120 mcg/mL is above the line, so start NAC.
items.md: Example: 8 h, 120 mcg/mL is above the line, so start NAC.

notes:
The nomogram predicts hepatotoxicity risk after a single acute ingestion; if time of ingestion is unknown or ingestion is chronic, do not rely on it. Start NAC without waiting if presentation is late or the level is unavailable and ingestion is significant.

After 24 hours the nomogram is not used: 4.7 mcg/mL is only where the treatment line ends, not a safe cutoff. Get AST/ALT; a detectable level or elevated AST/ALT guides NAC, per protocol or poison control.

title: Acetaminophen Toxicity

items.text: In overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows — this is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.

emphasis.text: In overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows — this is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.

items.md: **In overdose, glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows — this is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.**

notes:
NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine. Tie this directly back to the "toxic metabolite" bullet from Lecture 1’s drug metabolism section.

Ask: "What is the danger of a cold-and-flu product on top of regular acetaminophen?" Look for: unintentional double dosing from combination products.

title: The Hidden Acetaminophen Overdose

items.text: A patient takes acetaminophen regularly for chronic back pain. For a cold, they also start an over-the-counter combination cold-and-flu medication.
items.md: A patient takes acetaminophen regularly for chronic back pain. For a cold, they also start an over-the-counter combination cold-and-flu medication.

items.text: Ask yourself:  What is the hidden danger in this combination?

emphasis.text: What is the hidden danger in this combination?

items.md: **Ask yourself:** **What is the hidden danger in this combination?**

items.text: Clinical pearl:  Many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury. Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.

emphasis.text: In acetaminophen overdose, hepatotoxicity results primarily from which mechanism?

title: Answer

items.text: Why:  NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione, accumulates once glutathione stores are exhausted in overdose, causing hepatocyte injury — which is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.
items.md: **Why:** NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with glutathione, accumulates once glutathione stores are exhausted in overdose, causing hepatocyte injury — which is why N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) is the antidote.

title: How NSAIDs Work
notes: Say: "NSAIDs inhibit COX, so less arachidonic acid becomes prostaglandins and thromboxane. That gives less pain, inflammation and fever."

title: NSAIDs Block COX and Prostaglandin Synthesis

items.text: NSAIDs Block COX and Prostaglandin Synthesis
items.md: NSAIDs Block COX and Prostaglandin Synthesis

items.text: Pathway: arachidonic acid is converted by COX to prostaglandins and thromboxane A2.
items.md: **Pathway:**  arachidonic acid is converted by COX to prostaglandins and thromboxane A2.

items.text: Effect: reduced prostaglandins give analgesia, antipyresis and anti-inflammation.
items.md: **Effect:**  reduced prostaglandins give analgesia, antipyresis and anti-inflammation.

items.text: Adverse effects: GI injury, platelet inhibition and renal effects.
items.md: **Adverse effects:**  GI injury, platelet inhibition and renal effects.

items.text: Less prostaglandin: pain and fever fall
items.md: Less prostaglandin: pain and fever fall

notes:
Explain the COX step first; every NSAID shares this mechanism, and the side effects follow from losing protective prostaglandins.

Say: "NSAIDs inhibit COX, so less arachidonic acid becomes prostaglandins and thromboxane. That gives less pain, inflammation and fever."

title: COX-1 vs. COX-2

items.text: Maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow
items.md: Maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow

items.text: Inhibition contributes to GI and renal adverse effects
items.md: Inhibition contributes to GI and renal adverse effects

items.text: Induced mainly at sites of inflammation
items.md: Induced mainly at sites of inflammation

items.text: Selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity
items.md: Selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity

notes:
Stress this is a simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation — COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.

Say: "COX-1 is the housekeeper: stomach lining, platelets, kidney. COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation."

title: COX-1 vs. COX-2: Constitutive vs. Inducible

items.text: COX-1 vs. COX-2: Constitutive vs. Inducible
items.md: COX-1 vs. COX-2: Constitutive vs. Inducible

items.text: COX-1: constitutive; gastric mucosa, platelets, kidney.
COX-2: inducible in inflamed tissue; pain, swelling, fever.
items.md: **COX-2:**  inducible in inflamed tissue; pain, swelling, fever.

items.text: Nonselective NSAIDs block both, so GI injury is common.
items.md: **Nonselective NSAIDs**  block both, so GI injury is common.

items.text: Celecoxib spares COX-1 at therapeutic doses.
Nonselective NSAIDs block both COX-1 and COX-2 → GI and renal risk
items.md: Nonselective NSAIDs block both COX-1 and COX-2 → GI and renal risk

notes:
COX-1 keeps protective prostaglandins; COX-2 is induced by inflammation. Selectivity trades anti-inflammatory benefit against GI and platelet protection.

Say: "COX-1 is the housekeeper: stomach lining, platelets, kidney. COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation."

Know: Nonselective NSAIDs block both, which is why GI injury is common.

items.md: Ibuprofen — common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain

title: COX-2 Selective Inhibition: Celecoxib

items.text: Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.

emphasis.text: Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.

items.text: GI effects: lower risk of ulcer/bleeding than nonselective NSAIDs.
items.md: GI effects: lower risk of ulcer/bleeding than nonselective NSAIDs.

items.text: Cardiovascular risk: COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.

emphasis.text: Cardiovascular risk: COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.

items.md: **Cardiovascular risk: COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.**

items.text: Renal effects: similar renal risk to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.
items.md: Renal effects: similar renal risk to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.

notes:
This is a classic "trade one risk for another" teaching point — better GI profile, but not a free lunch cardiovascularly or renally.

Say: "Celecoxib spares COX-1, so the GI risk is lower. The trade-off is lower PGI2 without a matching drop in TXA2, which raises cardiovascular risk. The kidney is still affected."

Five points to repeat if time runs short:

1. Prostaglandins drive inflammatory pain, and COX makes them.

2. Acetaminophen is central, with no real anti-inflammatory effect. Overdose means NAPQI, and the antidote is NAC.
